breadcrumb: Wall graphics that make the space your own
h1: Wall graphics that make the space your own
lead: Wall graphics can give an ordinary interior a sense of identity, whether the goal is one branded feature or a coordinated story across several rooms. Unlike a standalone sign, the wall itself becomes part of the composition. For New York offices, shops and hospitality spaces, Vision Graphics helps connect artwork with the way people use the room. Consider the viewing distance, furniture, lighting and wall condition together, then choose how much of the surface needs graphics to achieve the intended effect.

sections.html: Doors, switches, corners and shelving can cut through a graphic. Include them in the layout early instead of treating the wall as an empty canvas. Keep key text out of obstructed areas and use large image forms where the artwork will be seen from across a room.

Identify paint type and age where known, texture, patches and areas of moisture or damage. A surface assessment or material test may be needed before the specification is settled. Discuss expected removal and future repainting so the choice reflects how the space will evolve.

A reception logo, a values statement and a full-room image need different amounts of wall space. Compare a focused graphic with a larger printed design before deciding on coverage. For photography, check the original image quality at the intended scale and confirm usage rights. Plan panel joins and keep faces, small text and other critical details away from corners or interruptions.

Coverage, material, artwork preparation, panel count and the condition of the wall affect the quote. Tall areas, stairs, fixed furniture, restricted work hours and removal of existing graphics can add site work. Confirm whether wall preparation, furniture movement, installation and later removal are included. A proposed display period does not by itself establish how a material will behave on a particular wall.

sections.h2: What to send for a wall-graphics quote
sections.html: Provide a wide photo, close-up surface photographs and approximate wall dimensions. Mark doors, switches, shelves and any areas that will be hidden by furniture. Include the artwork or image source, paint details if known, the project address or ZIP, desired display period and target date. Tell us whether the wall is newly painted or whether existing graphics need removal.

items.p: Use coordinated imagery, color or patterns across larger areas. Review the substrate, artwork scale, panel layout and installation access.
Apply individual words, icons and shapes while retaining the wall color. Fine details and letter size need production review.
Combine a logo or short message with a limited graphic area where a full-wall treatment would overwhelm the room.
Consider printed panels when a separate display surface better suits the brief. Confirm panel construction, attachment and the condition of the supporting wall.

items.q: Can graphics cover a textured wall?
items.a_html: Texture can affect adhesion and appearance. Share close-up photos and allow for material and surface review before selecting a method.

items.q: Do I need a mural or a smaller graphic?
items.a_html: Choose the amount of coverage that serves the room. A focused logo or statement can be more effective than filling every available surface.

items.q: Can wall graphics be removed without damaging the paint?
items.a_html: Removal depends on the material, paint, preparation, wall condition and how long the graphics remain in place. Explain removal expectations before material selection. Damage-free removal should not be assumed; any surface test and repair responsibilities should be agreed as part of the scope.

items.q: How soon can graphics go on a newly painted wall?
items.a_html: Provide the paint product, application date and the proposed graphic material. The project team should review the relevant preparation and curing guidance before scheduling installation. There is no single waiting period that fits every paint and graphic combination.
